extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans of television and improvisational comedy, and researchers of TV formats
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style informational article describing the American television improv series Whose Line Is It Anyway?, its format, performers, games, production history, and broadcast details. Useful for understanding the show's structure and the skills/production elements it emphasizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to create characters, scenes, and songs on the spot
rubrics_metrics.description: The show consists of a panel of four performers who create characters, scenes, and songs on the spot, in the style of short-form improvisation games.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topics for the games are based on either audience suggestions or predetermined prompts from the host, who sets up a game and situation that the performers would improvise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-form improvisation style (brevity and variety)
rubrics_metrics.description: The program uses a 'short-form' approach to improv — many varied, concise games rather than extended long-form scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The style of the games was varied; some games became common while others faded. The short-form approach introduced improv to mass audiences but received criticism from some improv actors who viewed it as not the 'be-all and end-all' of improv.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to work from audience suggestions and prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Games are often driven by studio audience suggestions or written prompts submitted in advance and selected by production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers must incorporate spontaneous topics supplied live (or pre-selected) into scenes and games; some games require rapid-fire incorporation (e.g., Scenes from a Hat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility across performance skills (singing, dancing, impressions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to improv, performers are tested on other skills such as singing, dancing, or impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whose Line features a number of musical games with live backing music; performers who cannot sing may adapt (e.g., spoken-word delivery), while others (like Wayne Brady) excel at musical numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humorous banter and ensemble chemistry
rubrics_metrics.description: The show is marked by humorous banter among the performers and host and by the chemistry between regulars and guests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Between games performers remain in seats and engage in banter; strong comic rapport enhances episode quality and audience enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proficiency in core game formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain games are recurring and form the backbone of the series' format (e.g., Scenes from a Hat, Greatest Hits, Props, Let's Make a Date, Weird Newscasters, Duet, Helping Hands, Questions Only).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers are expected to be familiar with the rules and conventions of these core games; the show included many other games brought from the British original or created for the US version, and some games were retired if not well received or if performers were reluctant to play them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to perform in both full-cast and reduced-cast games
rubrics_metrics.description: Some games feature all four performers while others use fewer; performers must adapt to different group sizes within an episode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When not involved in a game performers remain seated and may need to quickly enter or support scenes; quick transitions and awareness are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of playful, arbitrary scoring and show-as-gimmick
rubrics_metrics.description: The host awarded arbitrary point values after each game; the points were purely decorative and served no practical purpose — 'the show where everything's made up and the points don't matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing is a production/format convention: comedic, non-competitive judging and arbitrary selection of 'winners' who receive a light-hearted 'prize' (e.g., play a game with the host or sit out).

rubrics_metrics.name: End-of-episode theatricality (winner's bit and credits performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the conclusion a winner or winners are chosen arbitrarily and either play a game with the host or the cast perform a comedic reading of the credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later seasons used themed credit readings tied to successful jokes earlier in the show; performers must be able to execute a short, planned comedic bit to close the episode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production standards regarding music and accompaniment
rubrics_metrics.description: The show features resident musicians providing live backing music for musical games; occasionally pre-recorded music was used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordination with musicians is required for timing and musical improv; presence of live music affects pacing and performance choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience reception and iterative format pruning
rubrics_metrics.description: Some games were only played once or twice because they were not well received by audiences or because performers were reluctant to perform them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers retained and repeated games that resonated with audiences (eight games appeared at least once in every season), showing that audience reaction and performer comfort drive long-term format choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with broadcast content standards (censorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in broadcast standards (UK vs US prime time) required stricter censoring of both language and content on the US series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers and producers must adapt material to meet network censorship rules and standards for the show's airing time and market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility for guest and celebrity performers
rubrics_metrics.description: The series often featured celebrity guests who might not have an improv background but still participated in some games; the revival added a 'special guest' fifth player.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers need to be able to work with non-improvisers and adjust games to include celebrity guests, sometimes changing game selection or pacing to accommodate them.
